title: Number("") and Number(" ") both equal 0
assumption: An empty or blank string can't be converted to a valid number -- it should fail or return NaN.

input.description: Converting a form field or query-string parameter that the user left blank, using `Number(value)` as a validation/conversion step.

what_goes_wrong: A blank form field, passed through `Number()` as part of 'sanitize to a number', becomes the perfectly valid number 0 instead of failing validation, so an unanswered quantity/price/age field silently records as zero rather than being rejected as missing.
why: The ECMAScript string-to-number grammar defines the empty string (and a string containing only whitespace, since leading/trailing whitespace is trimmed first) as a valid `StringNumericLiteral` whose value is 0 -- this is an explicit rule in the spec, not an accidental byproduct of trimming. `parseInt` and `parseFloat`, by contrast, both return `NaN` for the same inputs, because they don't follow this grammar rule.

repros.expected_output:
'' -> ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: ''
'   ' -> ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '   '

fix: Check for an empty/whitespace-only string explicitly before calling `Number()` on user input; don't rely on it to reject blanks, since by spec it treats them as a valid zero.

sources.title: ECMA-262: ToNumber applied to the String type (StringNumericLiteral)

test_cases.note: A numeric-field validator must treat an empty string as missing, not silently accept it as zero.
